rows.sanctuary_meaning: Something already learned, reshaped so it can be handed to someone who has not yet learned it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin lectio (a reading, a reading-aloud), from legere (to read, gather); something learned and shaped into a form that can be read out and taught again.

rows.definition: A single written sign, and a written message sent to one person. Both are marks made to be read by another.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A single mark and a message sent to one reader share a word because both are marks made with someone else's reading in mind.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin littera (a letter of the alphabet; in the plural, an epistle), of disputed further origin, perhaps borrowed from a Greek word for a tablet; a single written sign, and a written message, are the same word because both are marks made to be read by another.

rows.definition: A degree on a scale, and the flatness of a plane. Both name a position measured against a fixed reference.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A position measured against a fixed reference, whether the reference is a scale of degree or the plain flatness of the ground.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin libella (a small balance, a level), a diminutive of libra (scale, balance), via Old French livel; a degree on a scale and the flatness of a plane are the same word because both are measured against a fixed reference.

rows.definition: The whole stock of words a mind or a system has, with their meanings. A lexicon is a vocabulary that knows itself.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A vocabulary that knows itself — not just the words a mind holds, but the meanings kept alongside them.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek lexikon (of words), from lexis (word, speech), from legein (to speak); the whole stock of words a mind or system holds along with their meanings.

rows.definition: One who keeps a collection so others can find what they need in it. The librarian's work is retrieval, not ownership.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The work here is retrieval, never ownership — a collection kept so that whoever needs something in it can actually find it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin liber (book; originally the inner bark of a tree, written on before papyrus reached Rome), with an agent suffix; one who keeps a collection so others can find what they need in it, without owning it.

rows.definition: The condition of a thing that maintains itself and can end. Also the whole span of one such thing, from beginning to end.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The atom folded into every lifecycle this house names — a thing that is not just present but moves through stages, is tended for a while, and is eventually let go.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English lif (life, existence), from Proto-Germanic liba, related to libban (to live), from a root meaning to remain, continue; the condition of a thing that maintains itself and can end.

rows.definition: The whole course of a thing from beginning to end. A lifecycle names the stages a thing must pass through.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The stages a thing must pass through named as one continuous course, from its first moment to its last.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English lif (life) joined to Greek kyklos (circle, wheel), via Latin cyclus; the whole course of a thing, run as one turning circle from beginning to end.

rows.definition: What makes seeing possible. Also of little weight — the same word for illumination and for ease.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Two old words wear one spelling now — what makes seeing possible, and what carries little weight — and neither sense explains the other.
rows.historical_meaning: Two distinct Old English words share this one spelling: leoht (brightness), from a root meaning to shine; and leoht (not heavy), from a separate, unrelated Proto-Indo-European root for lightness and nimbleness.

rows.definition: Resembling, without being the same. The word that compares while keeping the two apart.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A comparison that keeps two things apart even while drawing them close — resemblance is claimed, sameness is not.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English gelic (similar, alike), from ge- (a collective prefix) + lic (body, form); the word that compares two things by their shared form while keeping them apart.

rows.definition: The point past which a thing may not go. A limit can protect or constrain, and the same line does both depending on which side you stand.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The same line protects from one side and constrains from the other, and which it is doing depends entirely on where someone stands.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin limes (a boundary path, a frontier); the point past which a thing may not go, protecting or constraining depending only on which side of the line one stands.

rows.definition: A path of no width, and one row of written words. Also a descent of related beings, one after another.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A path with no width of its own, a row of written words, and a descent of kin one after another — three things sharing a name because each is a single thread followed from one end to the other.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin linea (a linen thread, a line drawn with one), from linum (flax); a path of no width, one row of writing, and a descent of kin all take their name from the drawn thread.

rows.definition: A line of descent, each carrying something from the one before. A lineage is continuity across instances rather than within one.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Continuity carried across separate instances rather than held within just one — each descendant keeps something of the one before it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin linea (a line, a thread), via Old French lignage; a line of descent, each carrying something from the one before, continuity across instances rather than within one.

rows.definition: Proceeding in a straight line, one step per step. Linearity is an assumption more often than an observation.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: An assumption reached for more often than it is actually observed — most things that look linear are only linear over a short enough stretch.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin linearis (of a line), from linea (a line, thread); proceeding one step at a time along a straight path — an assumption more often than an observation.

rows.definition: A single connection between two things, and the means of crossing it. One ring of a chain, useful only because it holds two others.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One ring of a chain, worth nothing on its own — its whole use is in holding two others that would otherwise stay apart.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse hlenkr (a link of a chain), related to Old English hlence (a ring of mail armour); one connection between two things, useful only because it holds two others.

rows.definition: A compound fragment naming a pass over links. Not an English word; flagged for the mis-cut band.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A fragment naming a pass over links, kept in the record as evidence of a cut that landed wrong rather than repaired into a word it never was.

rows.definition: Of the ranked naming system for living things — kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. A structure of nested belonging.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A structure of nested belonging, where every rank sits inside the one above it and holds every rank below.
rows.historical_meaning: Latinised from Linnaeus, the surname a father chose from Swedish lind (a linden tree) that grew on the family's land; the adjective names the ranked kingdom-to-species system the naturalist who bore it devised in the 18th century.

rows.definition: An ordered enumeration of things. First the strip of cloth at an edge - the border became the record written along it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A record that began as the border it was written along — the edge and what was written on it became, over time, one and the same word.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French liste (a border, a strip, an edging), of Germanic origin, related to Old English list (a hem, border); the strip at a garment's edge once carried a written record, and the border became the word for the record itself.

rows.definition: To attend with the ear — hearing chosen, not merely happening.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Hearing that was chosen rather than merely happening — the attention is the whole difference between listening and simply being within range of a sound.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English hlysnan (to listen), from Proto-Germanic hlusinojan, related to hlust (hearing), from a Proto-Indo-European root for hearing; hearing chosen and attended to, not merely happening.

rows.definition: That which waits to be told and answers when it is. Listening is a readiness, not an act.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A readiness rather than an act — nothing happens until it is told something, and then it answers.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English hlysnan (to listen), with an agent suffix; that which waits to be told and answers only when it is, a readiness rather than an act.

rows.definition: That which enumerates what is present. A lister's honesty is whether it prints its zeros.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Honesty here is measured by one habit alone: whether the zeros get printed along with everything else.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French liste (a border, a strip that carried a record), with an agent suffix; that which enumerates what is present, honest exactly to the degree it prints its zeros.

rows.definition: Happening now rather than recorded. Also carrying current — both mean a thing presently in effect.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Presently in effect, whether the sense is a broadcast happening now or a wire carrying current — both mean the thing is active, not merely stored.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English libban/lifian (to live, be alive), from Proto-Germanic libjan, related to lif (life); happening now rather than recorded, and, of current, a force presently in effect.
